clue.text: Cherry wore white for this occasion according to Housman

definitions.text: Cherry wore white for this occasion according to Housman

parts.words: Cherry wore white for this occasion according to Housman
parts.note: Housman's poem 'Loveliest of trees' has the cherry hung with bloom and wearing white for a spring church season

explanation.surface: A literary quiz question about a tree in blossom in a famous poem.
explanation.walkthrough: A.E. Housman's A Shropshire Lad opens 'Loveliest of trees, the cherry now' and has it 'wearing white for Eastertide'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem names the festival season when the blossoming tree dresses in white.

clue.text: Painter's simple yet typical show

definitions.note: read as 'Painter is', so the definition is a painter

indicators.note: to show is to display, so the letters are on view inside the words yet typical

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses an artist's exhibition as plain and predictable.
explanation.walkthrough: William Etty was an English painter of nudes; 'show' signals the letters on view across 'yET TYpical'.
explanation.definitionFit: William Etty was a nineteenth-century English artist.

clue.text: Kind of mail order activity

definitions.meaning: a kind is a type or variety
post office staff put letters in order by destination

explanation.surface: Describing a type of business that sells by post.
explanation.definitionFit: A type or variety, and also the arranging of letters into bundles at a post office.

clue.text: Serving needs when changing for the theatre.

indicators.note: changing means altering, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Staff at a restaurant must change before a night at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when changing' reworks the letters of SERVING NEEDS; the definition is formal clothes worn for a night out at the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal attire is what people traditionally wore for a night at a play.

clue.text: Act is transformed by it — understood!

indicators.note: transformed means changed in form, so the letters of act and it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A performance is changed by something, and suddenly it all makes sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is transformed by' rearranges ACT and IT together.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit agreement is implied and understood without being spoken.

clue.text: The foreign campanologist produces a pistol

parts.note: der is German for 'the'
a campanologist rings church bells, so is a bell-ringer

explanation.surface: A foreign bell-ringer pulls out a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: A campanologist is a bell-ringer; 'The foreign' gives DER, the German for 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: A derringer is a small, short-barrelled handgun.

clue.text: So would the fighter fire

parts.note: this word placed before 'fire' names a famous British fighter plane, and also means to fire out from the mouth

explanation.surface: A remark about how a fighter pilot would shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: Put this word before 'fire' and you get the Spitfire, the British fighter plane of the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined to the word fire it names the wartime fighter aircraft.

clue.text: Made by Old Moore prior to speech

parts.note: pre- is a prefix meaning before
diction is manner of speech

explanation.surface: Something an almanac maker said before a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Moore's Almanack is a long-running British annual famous for forecasting the year's events.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Moore's almanac is known for its forecasts of coming events.

clue.text: Dance, Jack, before everyone returns

parts.note: a jack tar is a sailor, so jack gives tar
ante is Latin for before

indicators.note: returns means the word for everyone comes back the other way

parts.note: everyone means all

explanation.surface: A sailor dances before everyone comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns ALL into LLA at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarantella is a fast Italian folk dance.

clue.text: In miles ten short of Babylon

definitions.text: In miles ten short of Babylon

parts.words: In miles ten short of Babylon
parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'How many miles to Babylon?' answers with a number of seventy, and this is ten fewer

explanation.surface: A traveller is ten miles away from Babylon.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme goes 'How many miles to Babylon? Three score and ten', so ten short of that distance is sixty.
explanation.definitionFit: Sixty, ten less than the rhyme's seventy miles to Babylon.

clue.text: Tolerate a honey lover

definitions.meaning: to tolerate is to put up with
the animal famous for raiding hives for honey

explanation.surface: Putting up with someone with a sweet tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: Endure, and also the big animal that famously loves honey.

clue.text: Our Dickensian is known to more than one

definitions.meaning: a Dickens novel title opens with 'Our'
a person two people both know

explanation.surface: A Dickens character is familiar to several people.
explanation.walkthrough: Our Mutual Friend is Dickens's last completed novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A person known in common by two others, and the Dickens novel title.

clue.text: Dirt is awkward, but one gets on to another economic problem

indicators.note: awkward means clumsy or out of place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Dirt is a nuisance, but one moves on to another financial issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' rearranges the letters of 'Dirt is'; 'gets on to another' is the link joining the pieces to the definition, how goods are shared out in an economy.
explanation.definitionFit: How wealth and goods are shared out is a central question in economics.

clue.text: He's bound to learn in time

definitions.text: He's bound to learn in time

parts.words: He's bound to learn in time
parts.note: a trainee tied by an indenture to a master to learn a trade over a set period

explanation.surface: Someone is sure to pick things up eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' means legally tied by indenture, not 'certain'.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainee indentured to a master craftsman for a term to learn a trade.

clue.text: Midas touch in post-war fiction

definitions.meaning: King Midas turned everything he touched to gold, so a digit with that power

explanation.surface: A golden touch appearing in a novel from after the war.
explanation.definitionFit: A gilding digit like Midas's, and Ian Fleming's Bond novel of 1959.

clue.text: Failing in all but Agriculture?

parts.note: British slang for failing an exam is a farming word, which in farming means working the soil

explanation.surface: A student failing every subject except farming.
explanation.walkthrough: In old British student slang to 'plough' an exam is to fail it; only in agriculture is it a pass.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for flunking exams, and literally tilling the fields.

clue.text: Movement of a neat mini — lifeless ?

indicators.note: movement means the letters are moved around

explanation.surface: A tidy little car moves, though it seems dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement of' rearranges A NEAT MINI; the Mini is a small British car.
explanation.definitionFit: Without life, like an object rather than a creature.

clue.text: Adjust a nut that is loose

indicators.note: adjust means rearrange, so the letters of nut are moved

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: Tightening or loosening a nut that has come free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adjust' turns NUT into UNT; 'loose' is a verb, to set free.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose a knot or a horse is to unfasten it.

clue.text: Recommendation for the horseman

definitions.meaning: a jury may add a note of advice to its verdict
one who sits astride a horse

explanation.surface: Advice for someone on horseback.
explanation.definitionFit: An addition to a verdict recommending something, and a person on horseback.

clue.text: First bootless errand boy ?

parts.note: on the first of a spring month people are sent on pointless errands as a prank

explanation.surface: Describing the original messenger who went unshod.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bootless' means futile, not shoeless; 'First' is the first of the month, the day for sending people on fools' errands.
explanation.definitionFit: A dupe sent on a pointless errand on the first day of the month of pranks.

clue.text: Useful for making ends neat

parts.note: a small curved cutting tool used to trim the tips of the fingers

explanation.surface: Advice on tidying up loose ends.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'ends' are fingertips.
explanation.definitionFit: Small curved blades for trimming the fingertips.

clue.text: How to start a meal, or this fight

explanation.surface: A dinner that ends in a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase for tucking into food, and a short brawl.

clue.text: Speculate on a letter from abroad

parts.note: to speculate is to gamble, to bet

explanation.surface: Gambling on post arriving from overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'letter from abroad' is the second letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The second letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: The boss is forced into a shirt

definitions.meaning: a boss is a raised ornamental knob
a detachable fastener pushed through shirt front holes

explanation.surface: The employer is made to dress formally.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised knob or boss, and a fastener pushed through a shirt.

clue.text: One who played upon the Moor

definitions.text: One who played upon the Moor

parts.words: One who played upon the Moor
parts.note: the villain who manipulated Othello in Shakespeare's tragedy

explanation.surface: Someone who played games on a moorland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'played upon' means manipulated, and 'the Moor' is Othello.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's ensign deceived and manipulated him.

clue.text: Fight intended, we hear, for the parapet

parts.note: a battle is a fight

indicators.note: we hear says the word is taken by its sound alone

parts.note: intended means meant

explanation.surface: Planning a fight to defend the castle walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns MEANT into its sound-alike MENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A notched defensive wall along the top of a castle.

clue.text: Work for Shaw deserting a Bronte character

indicators.note: deserting means leaving, so these letters go from the name

parts.note: Catherine Earnshaw in Emily Bronte's Wuthering Heights
taken as written

explanation.surface: Writing for Shaw rather than for a Bronte heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: Catherine and Hindley Earnshaw are in Wuthering Heights; 'deserting' drops SHAW.
explanation.definitionFit: To gain something through labour.

clue.text: Used to record details of minutes

definitions.meaning: the clock pointer that counts the seconds within each minute

explanation.surface: Old notes kept to write up meeting minutes.
explanation.definitionFit: Previously owned, and the clock hand counting off parts of a minute.
